fatal_errors: The proposal reduces component-level effective density through porosity rather than reducing the alloy's material density, so it does not establish retention of comparable intrinsic mechanical properties.

An open lattice tested on a nominal external-area basis will generally have lower apparent yield strength than a fully dense specimen unless component geometry, load path, and normalization are carefully redefined.
The cited evidence concerns LPBF synthesis of WTaMoNbV and provides no support for HfMoTaTiZr lattice structures retaining strength or creep resistance near 1000 °C.
The intervention and mechanism do not reconstruct the Cr-addition, solid-solution-hardening, and reticulated Laves-phase hypothesis.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses mass reduction and mentions room-temperature and 1000 °C testing, but it is scientifically and evidentially remote from the target. The target adds 4.2 at.% Cr by vacuum arc melting, producing about 3.8–4 vol.% of a reticulated Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves phase. Strengthening is attributed to Cr-induced lattice distortion and dislocation density, while the interconnected phase hinders cracks and preserves plasticity, yielding approximately 13.5% higher yield strength and 20.6% higher fracture strain. None of these intervention, structure, mechanism, or quantitative outcomes is recovered. The proposed LPBF lattice is a creative alternative, and its paired testing plus explicit 10% rejection threshold gives some discriminability. However, loading boundaries, relative density, architecture dimensions, stress normalization, oxidation protection, dwell time, and creep stress are not defined. Most importantly, lower apparent density from voids is conflated with lower material density and retention of material strength. The sole citation supports only general additive manufacture of another refractory HEA, not the claimed architecture or high-temperature performance.
